transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-03-21
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Dmitri (Redwood SE), Priya (Atlas Head of ML), Evan (Atlas SRE), Sara (Atlas PM)

Summary:
Quick scoping for an Atlas AI POC focusing on latency/throughput SLOs: clarifying TTFT vs TPOT, p95/p99 targets, benchmark plan, dataset for replay, and timeline for a 1-week POC. Agreed to exchange sample prompts, run baseline bench and iterate on dedicated pool sizing.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we'll kick off, this is maya from Redwood, with dmitri our se, how's everyone?
[00:06] Priya: good, thanks, excited — trying to get the latency piece nailed down before we do the user-facing pilot.
[00:10] Evan: yeah hi, i'm evan from infra, i'll be watching the SLOs and the impact on our autoscaling budget.
[00:14] Sara: sara here, PM, scope is basically we need sub-second responses for chat and low cost per token.
[00:19] Dmitri: awesome, so high level i want to make sure we align on terminology — we often use TTFT and TPOT. small note, transcription might say t t f t, etc.
[00:27] Priya: yes can you define those again? we saw some docs where TPOT was called tpt..
[00:31] Dmitri: sure — TTFT = time to first token, that's the latency users perceive when the model starts responding. TPOT in our notes stands for time per token — basically per-token server-side latency once streaming has started. some teams call it TPT or "per-token latency". important because they stress different parts of the serving stack: startup cost, model init or KV cache warm, vs steady-state generation cost.
[00:53] Maya: and from a SLO POV we usually propose separate targets: TTFT p95 and p99, and TPOT p95/p99. that way you capture cold-start blips and also steady-state throughput.
[01:03] Priya: ok what numbers are realistic for, say, a 7B open model vs a 13B quantized variant?
[01:08] Dmitri: rough ballpark — on a good GPU config, TTFT p95 for a 7b optimized can be ~120-200ms, p99 ~250-350ms. for 13b quantized maybe p95 180-320ms, p99 350-550ms, depends on KV cache and whether we need to load weights (cold). TPOT per-token steady state usually in the 10-40ms range p95 depending on batch size and kernel perf. these are ballparks.
[01:34] Evan: that variance matters — we have a user-interaction requirement: 300ms perceived delay to keep conversation flow. so p95 TTFT needs to be under 300ms.
[01:42] Priya: our target is basically p95 < 200ms if possible, p99 < 400ms, otherwise the UX team will flag it. is that doable?
[01:50] Dmitri: it's aggressive but doable with right model variant and dedicated pool sizing, plus prefix caching. we should validate with your prompt set.
[01:57] Maya: ok let's talk measurement — how do we measure so both sides agree?
[02:01] Dmitri: measurement plan i propose: 1) replay your sample traffic at different concurrency levels; 2) measure TTFT and TPOT at p50/p95/p99; 3) run cold-start scenarios (empty KV cache, new worker spin-up); 4) run warm scenarios (warmed KV caches and hot workers); 5) capture tokenization overhead and network time. we'll provide the harness — it's a small python tool that replays and records timestamps per request/token.
[02:25] Priya: do you record timestamps client-side or server-side? we care about end-to-end perceived latency (client -> first token).
[02:30] Dmitri: both — we record client-side and insert server-side marks via header/tracing when available. that helps split out network vs server processing. if you have tracing (openTelemetry) we can correlate.
[02:39] Evan: we can add otel headers. also how do you compute percentiles? rolling windows? big windows?
[02:44] Dmitri: we compute p95/p99 over the complete run and also report 1-minute sliding-window percentiles to surface bursts. we'll export raw samples (csv) so you can recompute with your tooling.
[02:55] Sara: what about concurrency and batching? our real traffic spikes to ~120 concurrent users issuing token streaming; average tokens per request ~60.
[03:04] Dmitri: ok we'll run scenarios at concurrency 1, 10, 50, 120 to see scaling. batching behaves differently: with continuous batching we can increase throughput but TTFT can increase slightly at low QPS if batching waits for more tokens. we can config max-batch-wait-ms to tune.
[03:18] Priya: we have an internal cost target too — $0.0007 per token ideally, but that's flexible for POC.
[03:24] Maya: we'll include per-token cost estimates for each config. Redwood Optimize recommendations will suggest quantization/batching tradeoffs.
[03:30] Evan: one more — can you emulate user sessions for KV cache benefits? many of our prompts reuse context across a session so caching reduces TTFT a lot.
[03:38] Dmitri: yes we'll run sessionized traffic where we replay conversation threads to measure prefix & KV cache hit effects. cold starts vs warmed sessions will be part of the plan.
[03:46] Priya: measurement fidelity — i want to ensure transcription or labeling doesn't mess with metrics; are there known gotchas?
[03:51] Dmitri: yep a few: tokenization mismatches (different tokenizers change token counts), load generator's network bias if run from a different region, and inaccurate clock sync between client and server. we recommend NTP sync and server-side marks. also include model version pinning — small model changes can change per-token costs.
[04:08] Maya: on the SLOs itself — do you prefer a combined SLO (e.g., 95% of requests across endpoints under X) or per-route SLOs?
[04:15] Sara: per-route would be better — chat endpoints need tighter TTFT than background batch summarization.
[04:19] Dmitri: agreed. we'll propose per-route p95/p99 and a global budget for cost/throughput.
[04:24] Priya: timeline? how long for the bench and then for the POC?
[04:27] Maya: proposed: share traffic sample by 3/23, we run baseline bench 3/24-3/25, share results 3/25, then one week POC starting 3/27 with dedicated pool and config tuning.
[04:36] Evan: we can do the sample by 3/23. 1-week POC ok.
[04:39] Dmitri: for dedicated pool sizing — we'll propose a couple options: small (1 device), medium (2-4 devices), large (4-8 devices). we'll map your concurrency+tokens to qps and estimate throughput and cost.
[04:51] Priya: can you also include the expected TTFT/TPOT tradeoffs per sizing?
[04:54] Dmitri: yes, each candidate will show estimated p95/p99 for both metrics and cost.
[04:59] Sara: instrumentation — we'll want tracing links in the Redwood Console and per-route dashboards.
[05:03] Maya: yes console will show per-route p50/p95/p99, token counts, and cost. we'll add tracing hooks if you want deeper spans.
[05:10] Priya: one last question on fallbacks — if dedicated pool is overloaded will Redwood route to hosted or degrade?
[05:16] Dmitri: by policy you can do graceful fallback to a cheaper model variant or to hosted capacity; we log and surface those as events. we'll include a fallback policy proposal for the POC.
[05:24] Maya: great. recap: Redwood to run baseline benchmark with your prompts (Dmitri), Atlas to share traffic sample and goals (Priya/Evan), Maya to send security docs and pricing, schedule benchmark run 3/26 with SRE present.
[05:37] Priya: sounds good. thanks all.
[05:40] Evan: thanks.
[05:42] Sara: thanks, bye.

Ending notes: transcript has occasional mis-attributions and minor transcription errors. Attachments referenced: "atlas_prompts_sample.json" (customer), "redwood_bench_harness_v1.zip" (Redwood), "redwood-security-snapshot.pdf" (Redwood).
